plan.title: Paired treated vs control DE in 5 subjects
plan.analytical_narrative:
The input is a 12,000 gene x 11 column raw integer count table (counts.csv, STAR/featureCounts, no length correction, no transcript-level data) with a 10-row metadata table carrying subject and condition. The design is a within-subject paired design: 5 human blood subjects, each contributing one control and one treated sample. The research question — which genes respond to treatment within each subject — is answered by a paired differential expression test in which the subject enters the design as a blocking term, so the condition effect is estimated within subject and the (typically large) between-subject variation is removed from the residual.

T1S1 runs the sample structure QC before any test: DESeq2 size factors, library sizes, a blind variance-stabilizing transform, a PCA on the 500 most variable genes and a sample-distance heatmap, all labelled by both subject and condition. In a paired blood design PC1 is usually subject identity rather than treatment; that is expected and is exactly the reason for the blocked design. This step also verifies that the count matrix has 10 sample columns matching the 10 metadata rows (the profile reports 11 columns for counts.csv, one of which is the gene identifier column — the step must confirm this and report any sample present in one file but not the other before proceeding).

T1S2 fits DESeq2 with design ~ subject + condition on the raw integer counts, with an explicit reference level (control) and the contrast named as condition, treated vs control, so a positive log2 fold change means higher expression under treatment. Pre-filtering is minimal (>=10 counts in at least 5 samples, the smallest group size) and independent filtering at alpha 0.05 does the rest; log fold changes are shrunk with apeglm for ranking and plotting while the unshrunken estimate and its standard error are kept in the table. Because counts come from an aligner plus a counter with no bias model at quantification, the step also draws the GC-content and gene-length bias diagnostic; cqn and EDASeq are absent from this environment, so if a trend appears the step reports it as a limitation rather than silently correcting it. With 5 pairs, DESeq2 flags rather than replaces count outliers and sets those p-values to NA — the step reports the NA counts from the outlier flag separately from those from independent filtering.

T1S3 is the report: MA plot, dispersion plot, p-value histogram, per-subject paired expression traces for the top genes (which is what makes the within-subject claim visible rather than asserted), and a robustness check against an edgeR quasi-likelihood F-test on the same counts and the same blocked design, with the intersection treated as the high-confidence set. No enrichment step is planned: the question asks which genes respond, not which pathways, and gene-set analysis was not requested.

Power caveat to carry through the report: 5 pairs, 12,000 genes. The paired design buys real power over an unpaired 5-vs-5, but a null or near-null result at FDR 0.05 is a plausible outcome and must be reported as such rather than rescued with an unadjusted p-value cutoff.

flags.message: With counts from an aligner and a counter, no bias model runs at the quantification, thus a sample-specific effect of the GC content and of the gene length can remain in the counts, and such an effect adds a difference between samples that the between-sample normalization does not remove. Draw the diagnostic: for each pair of samples, or for each sample against the median sample, plot the log ratio of the counts against the GC content of the genes and against the gene length, and report a trend. For a 3' tag library, the count does not depend on the gene length, thus plot the GC content only. Conditional quantile normalization (cqn) and the GC-content normalization of EDASeq are the tools of record for the correction, and both are absent from this pool. If the diagnostic shows a trend, state it in the plan and ask for cqn, or for a new quantification with a bias-aware quantifier such as Salmon with its GC bias model. If the diagnostic shows no trend, state the check and continue.
